result:
A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the unlucky timing of two or more processes touching the same thing at once. With a shared log, that shows up as lines interleaved mid-line or lost when two writers overlap.

To avoid it, open the file in append mode and hold an exclusive lock while you write:

```sh
{
  flock 9
  printf '%s %s\n' "$(date -Is)" "$msg" >&9
} 9>>"$LOG"
```

The `>>` makes every write land at the current end of the file, so writers never overwrite each other. `flock` makes other writers wait until the block finishes, so even multi-line entries stay intact. The lock is released when the block ends and file descriptor 9 closes.

This only works if every script that writes to the log uses the same lock. `flock` can also be unreliable on NFS, so keep the log on a local filesystem.

If each entry is a single short line written by one `printf` or `echo` with `>>`, on Linux local filesystems that is already safe in practice without the lock. Never use `>`, or read-modify-rewrite the file, from concurrent writers.
